items.followUp: Define melting point and state two factors that affect it.

rubric.why: The definition depends on the condition at which a liquid boils.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid’s vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying this defining condition.

rubric.why: Boiling point changes with external pressure.
rubric.description: States the effect of pressure on boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct pressure trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions between molecules require more energy to overcome.
rubric.description: Relates stronger intermolecular forces to a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally elevate a liquid’s boiling point.
rubric.description: States that non-volatile impurities raise the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of impurities.

modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to atmospheric pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point, while decreasing external pressure lowers it.
Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have higher boiling points.
Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point.

items.followUp: State two defects of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model did not explain why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the stability defect, including the fate of revolving electrons.

rubric.why: The model did not account for the discrete spectral lines observed for atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the spectral defect.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom: revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: How does hydrogen bonding affect the boiling point and surface tension of water?

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding strengthens attractions between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them.
rubric.description: Explains that hydrogen bonding raises boiling point by strengthening intermolecular attraction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect on boiling point and its connection to stronger attraction.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding also affects other physical properties of molecules.
rubric.description: Names another physical property affected by hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming one valid additional property, such as surface tension, viscosity or melting point.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding strengthens the attraction between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher.
Hydrogen bonding also affects physical properties such as surface tension and viscosity.
